summary: Reports statistics gathered by the NIC's NCP implementation over roughly 100 hours of uptime: counts of incoming messages, host-host control messages and the sizes of outgoing messages. The author suggests that people building NCPs for servers should consider the results.

plainLanguage.summary: A server counted the kinds of messages it got for a few days. It shares the counts so people building similar servers can learn from them.

questions: what kinds of messages did early ncp servers see
how big were early arpanet messages
subtitle: Statistics on network message patterns from 100 hours of NCP operation.

tldr.problem: Network Control Program (NCP) designers had made assumptions about network message patterns and usage, but had never gathered empirical data to test those assumptions.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC (Network Information Center) kept detailed statistics on incoming messages, control opcodes, and outgoing message sizes over approximately 100 hours of continuous uptime, spanning both weekdays and weekends.
tldr.outcome: The data showed that half of all messages are control messages (ALL opcodes dominate), 95% of messages are very short, and while most data is in small messages, a significant fraction comes in large messages, likely file transfers.

facts.label: ALL opcode range
facts.value: 50% on weekends, up to 98% on busy weekdays

today: RFC 550 was the first systematic measurement of ARPANET message patterns. While the specific numbers are from 1973, the principle of measuring network behavior remains central to modern network design and optimization.

sections.title: Gathering the Data
sections.content: RFC 550 reports on statistics gathered by the NIC's Network Control Program (NCP) implementation over approximately 100 hours of operation, mostly during working hours. The NCP is the software that controls how a Host communicates over the ARPANET. L.P. Deutsch at PARC documented counts of incoming messages, incoming host-host control opcodes (the instruction codes in control messages), and the sizes of outgoing messages. While the statistics were reset each time the system came up, the data represents a substantial period of real network operation and usage patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC computer kept track of every message it received and sent for about 100 hours. The author notes it only took about half an hour of programming to collect this data, but no one had bothered to measure this before.

sections.title: Key Findings
sections.content: The data revealed several surprising patterns. The total numbers of incoming and outgoing messages were almost identical, with only about 5% more outgoing messages than incoming. Control opcodes accounted for slightly over half of all incoming messages. The ALL opcode (a basic control operation) dominated the control opcode statistics, accounting for anywhere from about 50% of opcodes on weekends to as much as 98% on busy weekdays. Almost all other opcodes were NOPs (no operations). No other opcode ever accounted for more than 5% of traffic. Message size statistics showed that 95% of all outgoing messages contained only 1 to 4 PDP-10 words (36-bit words) of data. However, when considering the total amount of data transmitted, only 75% came from messages of the smallest size, with the remaining data spread fairly evenly across larger message sizes, suggesting that file transfers and data operations did use larger messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages (checking that things are working) make up half of all messages. Almost all control messages are the simple ALL type. Most messages are tiny (1-4 words), but when you add up the total data, some of it comes in bigger chunks for file transfers.

sections.title: Lessons for NCP Design
sections.content: The author draws three major conclusions from this data. First, because half of all messages are control messages of the ALL type, NCP implementations should focus on processing control messages efficiently. Second, since 95% of messages are very short, elaborate buffering and queuing schemes are unlikely to provide significant benefits, because any gains in efficient IMP use would be swamped by overhead within the Host itself. Third, because a sufficiently large fraction of data comes in large messages (presumably file transfers), NCPs must also handle large transfers efficiently. An NCP that always sent single-character messages, for example, would not be satisfactory. The author notes that even those engaged in computer science had not previously found it necessary to confirm their hypotheses about network operation by experiment, and found it regrettable that these basic measurements had not been gathered earlier.
sections.plainLanguage: NCP designers should make control message handling fast, but don't need fancy buffering tricks for small messages. They do need to handle file transfers efficiently too. The author thinks it is sad that no one measured this before.
